HAEMATOLOGICAL__Lymphadenopathy:
Lymphadenopathy is sorted by two axes: localised vs generalised, and reactive vs malignant. Most is reactive — tender, mobile nodes draining a local infection, or generalised nodes from a systemic infection (EBV glandular fever, CMV, HIV, TB, toxoplasmosis) (see viral infections, tuberculosis, HIV). The job is to spot the malignant nodes: hard, fixed, matted, painless, >2 cm and persistent (>6 weeks), often with B symptoms (fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss) — lymphoma and leukaemia (see lymphoma, leukaemia), or metastatic carcinoma. A supraclavicular node is sinister — a left supraclavicular node (Virchow’s / Troisier’s sign) points to an intra-abdominal (gastric) malignancy. Examine all nodal areas plus the liver and spleen, and biopsy a persistent or suspicious node (see splenomegaly).
🚨Some nodes must be biopsied, not watched. A hard, fixed, matted, painless node, one >2 cm or persisting beyond 6 weeks, or any node with B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), needs an urgent excision / core biopsy for lymphoma (see lymphoma). A supraclavicular node is malignant until proven otherwise — a left supraclavicular (Virchow’s) node suggests gastric / intra-abdominal cancer, a right-sided one thoracic disease (see lung cancer). Generalised lymphadenopathy with hepatosplenomegaly and an abnormal blood count may be leukaemia (see leukaemia). And matted cervical nodes with weight loss and night sweats may be tuberculosis (see tuberculosis) — or lymphoma; the biopsy decides.

1Confirm & classify
🚩Lymphoma
  • Painless, rubbery, persistent nodes; B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss)
  • Alcohol-induced nodal pain and pruritus (Hodgkin); → excision / core biopsy (see lymphoma)
  • Generalised nodes ± hepatosplenomegaly
🚩Metastatic carcinoma
  • Hard, fixed, irregular node — a metastasis; find the primary
  • Left supraclavicular (Virchow’s / Troisier’s) → gastric / intra-abdominal; supraclavicular → thoracic (see lung cancer)
  • Cervical nodes → head & neck cancer (smoker / drinker)
🚩Leukaemia
  • Generalised nodes + hepatosplenomegaly + an abnormal blood count
  • CLL (elderly, lymphocytosis); ALL (children, blasts) (see leukaemia)
  • Look for bruising, pallor, infection (marrow failure)
🟠Serious infection
  • TB: matted cervical nodes, may caseate / form a sinus, weight loss (see tuberculosis)
  • EBV glandular fever, CMV, HIV seroconversion, toxoplasmosis (see viral infections, HIV)
  • Often tender / generalised with systemic features
🦠Reactive / local
  • Tender, mobile, soft nodes draining a local infection (tonsillitis, dental, skin) — the commonest
  • Resolve as the infection settles; a clear source is reassuring
  • Short-lived and self-limiting
🩺Other
  • Sarcoidosis (bilateral hilar), autoimmune disease (SLE, RA) (see sarcoidosis)
  • Drug reactions (e.g. phenytoin), Castleman’s disease
  • Consider when infection and malignancy are excluded
Reactive or malignant — and where? Tender, mobile nodes with a source are reactive. Hard, fixed, matted, painless, >2 cm or persistent nodes — especially supraclavicular or with B symptoms — are malignant until biopsy proves otherwise.

Texture and site triage it. Rubbery / painless generalised nodes with B symptoms are lymphoma; a hard fixed supraclavicular node is metastatic carcinoma; tender mobile nodes are reactive. When in doubt about a persistent node, biopsy.
3Assess & act
At the bedside — the node, all the regions, the spleen, the B symptoms
History & red flags
Duration and change, pain vs painless, B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), a local infective source, travel / TB / HIV risk, smoking & alcohol, medications, and pruritus / alcohol-induced pain
Examine
Node size, consistency, fixation, tenderness, matting and site (especially supraclavicular); examine all nodal regions, the liver and spleen, the skin, and the drainage area (throat, scalp, breast, abdomen)
Investigate
FBC + blood film, LDH, ESR / CRP; monospot / EBV serology, HIV test, and a chest X-ray (hilar nodes, TB); an ultrasound of a node, and an excision / core biopsy of any persistent or suspicious node; CT for staging / a primary; FNA of a suspected metastatic node
Act
Reactive nodes — treat the source and review. For a persistent, hard, fixed or supraclavicular node, refer urgently and biopsy; stage and treat lymphoma / leukaemia (haematology) or the primary cancer (oncology); treat TB / HIV / EBV on their pathways
Then — confirm the cause
Lymphoma → excision / core biopsyMetastatic carcinoma → FNA + imaging (find primary)Leukaemia → FBC + blood filmTuberculosis → node biopsy / cultureEBV glandular fever → monospot / EBV serologyReactive → observe / treat the source
The rules that carry it: reactive nodes are tender, mobile and resolve; malignant nodes are hard, fixed, painless, persistent or supraclavicular. Screen with FBC / film, LDH, monospot, HIV, CXR, and biopsy anything persistent or suspicious — the biopsy separates lymphoma, TB and metastasis.

HAEMATOLOGICAL__Splenomegaly:
Splenomegaly is graded by size and then by mechanism. A spleen enlarges towards the right iliac fossa, is dull to percussion, has a notch, moves with respiration, and you cannot get above it. Massive splenomegaly (crossing the midline to the RIF) has a short list: chronic myeloid leukaemia, myelofibrosis, and chronic malaria / visceral leishmaniasis (see myeloproliferative disorders, leukaemia, malaria). Moderate / mild splenomegaly is broad: infiltration (leukaemia, lymphoma, myeloproliferative), congestion from portal hypertension (cirrhosis), work hypertrophy from haemolysis (thalassaemia, spherocytosis) or infection (EBV, endocarditis, malaria) (see cirrhosis, thalassaemia). When the liver is also enlarged, work it up as hepatosplenomegaly (see hepatomegaly & splenomegaly); check for lymphadenopathy too (see lymphadenopathy).
🚨Three dangers. A big spleen can rupture — after trauma or spontaneously in an enlarged spleen (EBV, malaria) — causing shock, left-upper-quadrant pain and referred left shoulder-tip pain (Kehr’s sign) → resuscitate and urgent surgery; advise against contact sports in glandular fever. Massive splenomegaly that crosses the midline points to CML or myelofibrosis (or chronic infection) — send a blood film and JAK2 / BCR-ABL (see myeloproliferative disorders). And hypersplenism pools and destroys blood cells — the enlarged spleen can cause anaemia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia (pancytopenia) with the risk of bleeding and infection. Always look for the underlying malignancy and examine the nodes and liver (see lymphoma).

1Confirm & classify
🚩Splenic rupture
  • Trauma or spontaneous in an enlarged spleen (EBV, malaria) → shock
  • LUQ pain + left shoulder-tip pain (Kehr’s sign) → resuscitate + urgent surgery
  • Advise against contact sports in glandular fever
🚩Massive splenomegaly
  • Crosses the midline to the RIF — a short differential
  • CML (high WCC), myelofibrosis (teardrop cells), chronic malaria / kala-azar (see myeloproliferative disorders, malaria)
  • Send a blood film + JAK2 / BCR-ABL
🚩Haematological malignancy
  • Leukaemia (CML / CLL), lymphoma, myeloproliferative disease (see leukaemia, lymphoma)
  • Often with lymphadenopathy, B symptoms, abnormal counts (see lymphadenopathy)
  • Infiltration of the spleen; needs FBC / film ± marrow
🟠Portal hypertension
  • Cirrhosis / congestive splenomegaly — stigmata of chronic liver disease (see cirrhosis)
  • Part of a hepatosplenomegaly picture (see hepatomegaly & splenomegaly)
  • Confirm with LFTs and a portal-vein Doppler
🟠Haemolysis / infection
  • Haemolytic anaemias: thalassaemia, hereditary spherocytosis, sickle sequestration (children) (see thalassaemia, sickle cell disease)
  • Infection: EBV glandular fever, infective endocarditis, acute malaria
  • Reticulocytes, bilirubin, LDH, film, DAT; cultures
🩺Hypersplenism / other
  • Hypersplenism: pooling / destruction → pancytopenia
  • Felty’s (RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia), sarcoid, amyloid, storage disease (Gaucher’s)
  • Consider once the common causes are excluded
Size narrows it; mechanism confirms it. Massive (crosses the midline) = CML, myelofibrosis or chronic infection. Moderate splits into infiltration (malignancy), congestion (portal hypertension) and work (haemolysis / infection). Watch for rupture and hypersplenism.

Massive means marrow or chronic infection. A spleen that crosses the midline is CML, myelofibrosis or chronic malaria / kala-azar. Moderate splenomegaly with liver stigmata is portal hypertension; with jaundice and reticulocytosis it is haemolysis.
3Assess & act
At the bedside — confirm and grade the spleen, the liver, the nodes, the blood
History & red flags
B symptoms, bruising / bleeding / infections (hypersplenism), travel (malaria), trauma or LUQ / shoulder-tip pain (rupture), chronic liver disease, jaundice / anaemia, and a family history of haemolysis
Examine
Confirm the spleen (enlarges to the RIF, dull, notched, moves with respiration, can’t get above it); grade the size (massive = crosses the midline); examine the liver, lymph nodes, skin (bruising, jaundice) and for stigmata of liver disease
Investigate
FBC + blood film (blasts, teardrop cells, lymphocytosis, parasites), reticulocytes, bilirubin, LDH, DAT (haemolysis), LFTs, JAK2 / BCR-ABL, blood cultures / monospot / malaria films; an abdominal ultrasound (size, portal vein) ± CT; a bone marrow or node biopsy as indicated
Act
Treat the cause — haematology for leukaemia / lymphoma / myeloproliferative disease, manage portal hypertension and haemolysis, and treat infection (antimalarials, antibiotics). For splenic rupture, resuscitate and operate. Address hypersplenism; splenectomy in selected cases (with vaccination + prophylaxis)
Then — confirm the cause
CML / myeloproliferative → blood film + JAK2 / BCR-ABL (± marrow)Leukaemia / lymphoma → FBC / film + biopsyPortal hypertension → LFTs + USS / portal DopplerHaemolysis → reticulocytes + bilirubin + LDH + DATMalaria → blood filmsSplenic rupture → clinical / CT → surgery
The rules that carry it: confirm it is the spleen, grade the size (massive → CML / myelofibrosis / chronic infection), and get a blood film. Split moderate splenomegaly into infiltration, congestion and haemolysis / infection, and guard against rupture and hypersplenism.
